stories.headline: Denver City Council, mayor reach compromise adding $4 million for 2027 rent assistance
stories.summary:
The Denver City Council and Mayor Mike Johnston's office have reached a compromise that adds $4 million to next year's budget for the Temporary Rental and Utilities Assistance Program. The council approved the deal late in its Monday night meeting. It brings the total available for the program to $8.5 million in 2027, still below the $15 million the city plans to spend this year.

The council amendment adds $1.72 million to the fund, and the mayor's office said it plans to add $2.3 million more in the coming weeks. The money will come partly from the city's contingency fund and partly from several departments' service and supplies budgets. Councilwoman Serena Gonzales-Gutierrez, who sponsored the amendment, said the need far exceeds available funds. Only Councilmembers Amanda Sawyer and Kevin Flynn voted against it.

Johnston had originally proposed $4.5 million for the program. Next year will be the first since the pandemic without federal American Rescue Plan Act dollars to help pay for it. Earlier this month Johnston rejected a council letter seeking more investment, saying he wanted to see the results of a Harvard University study first.

The council also approved smaller amendments, including $300,000 for the Nest56 affordable housing complex and $200,000 for the Office of Children's Affairs to collect youth violence prevention data. After the compromise passed, Gonzales-Gutierrez withdrew a separate $5.5 million amendment.

stories.headline: Colorado voters back harsher penalties for fentanyl crimes
stories.summary:
Proposition 132, which would increase criminal penalties for possessing, selling or distributing fentanyl, appears poised to pass based on returns posted Wednesday. The measure had 52.8% yes votes to 47.2% no, a margin of about 130,000. It has gained ground since the first tally, which showed it trailing.

If enacted, the measure would make possession of any amount of fentanyl a felony and impose an eight-year mandatory minimum for distribution. It would require court-ordered treatment for people caught with less than a gram and make it harder for some defendants to receive reduced sentences. Supporters, including Advance Colorado, argue existing laws have not deterred distribution and that overdose deaths remain too high even though they have declined.

Opponents say the measure would punish people struggling with addiction, increase prison populations and could worsen the overdose crisis. They also warn mandatory sentences might discourage people from seeking treatment or reporting overdoses. Denver Mayor Mike Johnston said the city needs higher sentences but criticized the proposal for mandating treatment without providing resources, and for excessive penalties at the lowest distribution levels.

The Common Sense Institute reported synthetic opioid overdose deaths in Colorado have grown 17% since November 2024. The DEA's Rocky Mountain Field Division has seized nearly 3.2 million fentanyl pills and more than 92 kilograms of powder since Jan. 1.

stories.headline: Driver faces charges in deadly Commerce City motorcycle crash
stories.summary:
A driver is expected to face charges following a deadly motorcycle crash in Commerce City in the early hours of Wednesday morning. The Commerce City Police Department announced the expected charges in a social media post.

The department's announcement indicated that the crash resulted in a fatality involving a motorcyclist. Further details, including the identity of the victim, the driver's name and the specific charges, were not immediately available in the initial report.

Investigators are expected to release more information as the case proceeds. Readers are encouraged to follow Commerce City Police Department updates for additional details.

stories.headline: Business leaders weigh ballot measures as Amendment 87 holds razor-thin lead
stories.summary:
Colorado business leaders were closely watching ballot measures still being tallied Wednesday, particularly Amendment 87, which would replace the state's flat 4.4% income tax with a graduated system reaching beyond 8% for some higher incomes. As of late Wednesday afternoon it held a lead of about 0.4%. Analysts noted outstanding ballots from slower-reporting rural areas could shift the result.

Doug Friednash of Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck called the election a "political tsunami" and said Colorado is a deeper blue state. He praised Governor-elect Phil Weiser for opposing the amendment days before the election. Loren Furman, president and CEO of the Colorado Chamber of Commerce, said the measure would penalize small business owners and hurt competitiveness.

Voters appeared to have approved Proposition NN, which raises the amount of revenue the state can retain and spend under TABOR, with the funds directed to K-12 education. Leslie Oliver of the Denver Metro Chamber of Commerce said the chamber will work with lawmakers to ensure the money goes to teacher pay and smaller classrooms as promised, rather than to the General Fund. She said the chamber would also keep pressing for funding for roads and transportation infrastructure.

stories.headline: Convey ranks No. 5 among large companies on Denver Business Journal's 2026 Fast 50
stories.summary:
Convey, an enterprise software provider serving utilities and state and local governments, has been named to the Denver Business Journal's 2026 Fast 50 list of the fastest-growing private companies in the Denver area. It ranked fifth in the Large Business category, based on revenue growth from 2023 to 2025.

Founded in 1998, Convey describes itself as an engagement operating system for utilities and regulated industries, connecting core systems with automated workflows to manage customer communications. CEO Maulik Datanwala called the ranking a milestone reflecting the work of employees, customers and partners.

The recognition follows Convey's inclusion on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of fastest-growing private companies in America. Convey is a portfolio company of OceanSound Partners and Energy Impact Partners.

stories.headline: Colorado adds restaurants to Michelin Guide, bringing state total to 63
stories.summary:
The Michelin Guide has added more Colorado restaurants as anonymous inspectors expanded their reach across the Front Range and mountain communities. The guide debuted in Colorado in 2023 with a focus on Denver, Boulder and resort destinations. Recognitions now cover 63 Colorado eateries, including 10 Michelin-starred restaurants.

Three of the starred restaurants belong to Denver Chef Johnny Curiel, whose newest honoree, Milpero, joins Alma Fonda Fina and Mezcaleria Alma. Among the 15 most recently added are Annette in Aurora, praised for bistro-inflected fare, and Denver's Pig and Tiger and Rougarou, which draws on Cajun and Creole traditions.

Eleven additional restaurants earned recommended status, including Casa Juani in Boulder, Dân Dã in Aurora, Dear Emilia, Florence Supper Club, Heretík and Madeline in Denver, Four by Brother Luck in Colorado Springs, and Radicato in Breckenridge.

stories.headline: Avalanche goalie Scott Wedgewood 'trying to figure it out' after tough outings
stories.summary:
Colorado Avalanche goalie Scott Wedgewood was pulled from a 7-2 loss to the Columbus Blue Jackets on Tuesday after allowing four goals on nine shots. That followed a start in Nashville in which he gave up six goals on 35 shots in a 6-2 defeat. "I'm trying to figure it out," Wedgewood said.

Last season Wedgewood led the NHL in save percentage (.921) and goals-against average (2.02) in 45 games, and he and Mackenzie Blackwood shared the Jennings Trophy. This year he has made just five starts in the first 16 games, going 1-3-1 with an .867 save percentage. The Avalanche have lost their last four games.

Coach Jared Bednar said before the season that Blackwood would get every opportunity to be the No. 1 goalie, a decision Wedgewood supported. The 34-year-old said it has not been a bad year, just two bad games, and called it a mental challenge.

stories.headline: Blackhawks rookie eager to see Avalanche prospect Ilya Nabokov reach NHL
stories.summary:
Chicago Blackhawks rookie Roman Kantserov said he is eager to see his former KHL teammate, Avalanche goaltending prospect Ilya Nabokov, reach the NHL. The two played together for three seasons in the KHL and won the league title in 2023-24, when Nabokov was named Rookie of the Year and playoffs MVP.

Nabokov has begun his North American career with the Colorado Eagles of the AHL, posting a 4-2-1 record with a .931 save percentage and 2.11 goals-against average in seven starts, including a 32-save shutout in his first. Kantserov has six goals in his first 15 NHL games.

The timing of Nabokov's NHL opportunity is uncertain, as the Avalanche have Mackenzie Blackwood and Scott Wedgewood in net. His chance could come this season through injury or performance, or next year as the team faces salary cap decisions. Eagles teammates are using a translator app to help the 23-year-old acclimate.

stories.headline: Denver weather: cloudy, cool conditions with heavy mountain snow possible
stories.summary:
Denver will see mostly cloudy skies Wednesday with a high of 57 degrees and slightly breezy winds, according to the National Weather Service. A slight chance of rain is forecast for the evening, mostly before 8 p.m., with a low near 37 degrees overnight.

Significant precipitation is expected along the foothills and mountains south of I-70, where 3 to 10 inches of snow is possible. A quick system is expected to add snow to the central mountains and a light shower along the Palmer Divide.

Denver residents will need to keep waiting for the first snow of the season. Dry, mild conditions are forecast heading into the weekend, with Thursday returning to sunshine and highs in the upper 50s, and temperatures reaching up to 66 degrees over the weekend.

weather.notable: Nearly 6 degrees above the average high for this time of year.

topStory.headline: Democrats Win House and Senate in Midterm Sweep; Mississippi and Alaska Senate Races Remain Uncalled
topStory.summary:
Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the midterm elections, with victories in Republican-leaning and battleground states. According to Yahoo's account of Associated Press tallies, Democrats flipped seven Senate seats and hold 54 seats to the Republicans' 44, with contests in Alaska and Mississippi still undeclared. As of 5 a.m. ET Thursday, Democrats held 240 House seats to the GOP's 147, well past the 218-seat majority threshold, with 48 races still to be called. The party is on track for its largest House majority since 2008.

Among the Senate results, James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate seat there since 1988. Abdul El-Sayed beat Mike Rogers in Michigan and will be the first Muslim U.S. senator. Annie Andrews defeated Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, and Troy Jackson unseated Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, ending her three-decade tenure. Democrats also flipped seats in North Carolina (Roy Cooper), Ohio (Sherrod Brown), Iowa (Josh Turek) and Kansas (Adam Hamilton), while Sen. Jon Ossoff won reelection in Georgia. Among governors, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history in Georgia, Amy Acton became Ohio's first woman governor, and Gina Hinojosa became the first Democrat elected governor of Texas in nearly 40 years. Republican Byron Donalds was elected Florida's first Black governor.

The Mississippi Senate race between Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom remains too close to call. With about 96% of the vote counted, Colom led with 49% to Hyde-Smith's 48.9%, a margin of 1,138 votes out of more than 948,000 cast, according to the AP. County clerks have 10 days to certify the election. A Colom win would make him the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the state in decades. In Colorado, the 4th District race between Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert and Democrat Eileen Laubacher also remains tight.

Republican leaders and the president reacted to the losses. Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas called the results an "ass-kicking" and a "Watergate-level repudiation," citing high costs, tariffs and the length of the Iran war, and said Republicans did not do enough to address voters' economic pain. Vice President JD Vance wrote on X that the war was the reason for the losses. President Trump acknowledged that the eight-month-long Iran war hurt Republicans but defended it, saying, "you can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon." He signaled willingness to work with Democrats while indicating he would use his veto power.

Democrats are now weighing what the results mean for the party's direction. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the wins pave the way for a progressive candidate in the 2028 presidential race, and said he supports Congress acting against corruption in Washington while avoiding a question on impeachment. He reaffirmed support for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer but stopped short of urging candidates he backed to support them. In California's 11th District, Connie Chan conceded to fellow Democrat Scott Wiener in the race to succeed Rep. Nancy Pelosi. Remaining House calls, the Alaska and Mississippi Senate outcomes, and the Mississippi certification period will determine the final size of the Democratic majorities.
